fetched_contents.text: A Systematic Review of Criteria Used to Define Recovery from Sport-Related Concussion in Youth Athletes . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2019 Sep 1. Published in final edited form as: Br J Sports Med. 2017 Jul 22;52(18):1179–1190. doi: 10.1136/bjsports-2016-096551 Abstract Objective The Concussion in Sport Group guidelines recommend a multifaceted approach to help clinicians make return to sport decisions. The purpose of this study was to identify the most common multifaceted measures used to define clinical recovery from sport-related concussion in young athletes (high school and/or college level) and to summarise existing knowledge of criteria used to make return to sport decisions. Design Systematic review Data Sources The PubMed (MEDLINE), SPORTDiscus, and Embase electronic databases were searched from January 1, 2000 to March 1, 2017 by 3 independent reviewers. Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria: elementary, high school and college age groups, and a specific definition of clinical recovery that required two or more measures. Exclusion criteria: review articles, articles using the same sample population, case studies, non-English language, and those that used one measure only or did not specify the recovery measures used. Study quality Study quality was assessed using the Downs and Black Criteria. Results Of 2,023 publications, 43 met inclusion criteria. Included articles reported the following measures of recovery: somatic symptom resolution or return to baseline (100%), cognitive recovery or return to baseline (86%), no exacerbation of symptoms on physical exertion (49%), normalisation of balance (30%), normal special physical examination (12%), successful return to school (5%), no exacerbation of symptoms with cognitive exertion (2%), and normalisation of cerebral blood flow (2%). Follow-up to validate the return to sport decision was reported in 8 (19%) articles. Most studies were case-control or cohort (Level of Evidence 4) and had significant risk of bias. Conclusion All studies of sport-related concussion use symptom reports to define recovery. A minority of studies used multiple measures of outcome or had clearly defined recovery criteria, the most common being a combination of a self-reported symptom checklist and a computerized neurocognitive test. Future studies ideally should define recovery a-priori using objective physiological measures in addition to symptom reports. The majority of these are sport-related concussions.2 Although there is some ambiguity in the definitions of mild traumatic brain injury and concussion, the term concussion is generally used in sport-related injuries.3 Concussion occurs when sudden deceleration and rotational forces applied to the brain 4 trigger an acute and subacute pathophysiological metabolic response in the absence of gross brain lesions.5 Concussion results in somatic, cognitive and emotional symptoms, cognitive impairment, abnormal physical examination findings, behavioral issues, and sleep disturbance.6 Many patients with sport-related concussion recover within 7 – 10 days 7,8 although a recent study in adolescents, which defined recovery as normalisation of physiological, visual and balance function,9 reported that recovery typically required 3–4 weeks. The most widely accepted guidelines for return to sport are the Concussion in Sport Group (CISG) guidelines. The most recent are from the Berlin 5th International Conference on Concussion in Sport that recommend a multifaceted evaluation to include physical examination, neuropsychological testing, and a graded return to activity to help determine recovery from concussion. The latest CISG guidelines state that athletes should return to a baseline level of symptoms but do not provide definitions to establish when an athlete is fully recovered physiologically and ready to return to sport. Resolution of symptoms is recognised as a critical part of recovery but symptom reporting alone is problematic because athletes often under-report symptoms,10 some concussion-related symptoms are reported in populations without concussion,11 and symptoms are not specific to concussion.12 While the CISG guidelines recommend that symptom and cognitive recovery must occur before athletes can return to sport, actual clinical practice may differ.13 Buckley et al.14 found that 65% of athletic trainers used a multifaceted assessment to establish recovery from sport-related concussion while 11% used only one or no assessment tool when deciding on return to sport. The most frequently used assessments were symptom reports (92%), clinical examination (86%), computerized neuropsychological testing (74%), balance testing (65%), and the Standard Assessment of Concussion (SAC) (54%). An evidence-based definition of recovery from concussion is important given the risk of more severe consequences should repeat injury occur before resolution of the first concussion15 and increased awareness of possible long-term effects of concussion.16 The test-retest reliability and internal consistency of Immediate Post-concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT),17 the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test (BCTT),18 and the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT)19 have been reported on but not for other measures. fetched_contents.text: Treatment and Management of Prolonged Symptoms and Post-Concussion Syndrome - Sports-Related Concussions in Youth Most young people who sustain a concussion during active play or sports naturally progress from the injury event through a period of symptom resolution, followed by a return to full normal activities. As discussed in Chapter 3, in 80 to 90 percent of cases, individuals' symptoms resolve within 2 weeks (Makdissi et al., 2010; McClincy et al., 2006; McCrea et al., 2009, 2013; McCrory et al., 2013), although recovery within that period appears to be somewhat slower for adolescents ages 13 years through high school than for college-age athletes (Covassin et al., 2010; Eisenberg et al., 2013; Field et al., 2003; McClincy et al., 2006). In 10 to 20 percent of individuals, however, concussive symptoms persist for a number of weeks, months, or even years. These individuals may be said to be experiencing post-concussion syndrome (PCS). This chapter reviews the diagnostic definitions of PCS, potential early predictors of prolonged recovery, and the symptomatology and management of individuals with prolonged recovery or PCS. The chapter addresses those areas described in the statement of task that pertain to risk factors for PCS; the cognitive, affective, and behavioral changes that may occur during the subacute and chronic posttraumatic phases; and the treatment and management of PCS. The committee's charge did not include the development or recommendation of specific clinical practice guidelines. Given that, the chapter is limited to a review and discussion of the available literature on the treatment and management of individuals experiencing prolonged recovery from a concussion.1 DIAGNOSTIC DEFINITION Post-concussion syndrome is the persistence of a constellation of physical, cognitive, emotional, and sleep symptoms beyond the usual recovery period after a concussion. The World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10), defines PCS2 as > a syndrome that occurs following head trauma (usually sufficiently severe to result in loss of consciousness) and includes a number of disparate symptoms such as headache, dizziness, fatigue, irritability, difficulty in concentration and performing mental tasks, impairment of memory, insomnia, and reduced tolerance to stress, emotional excitement, or alcohol. (WHO, 2010, F07.2) The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) no longer contains a specific entry for “postconcussional disorder.” Instead, the fifth edition of the DSM captures persistent concussive symptoms under “neurocognitive disorder due to traumatic brain injury” (APA, 2013, pp. 624ff). The diagnostic criteria specify that the neurocognitive disorder must persist “past the acute post-injury period.” There is concern that the symptoms associated with the diagnostic criteria for PCS are nonspecific and that they frequently occur in the absence of head injury and in conjunction with other psychiatric conditions (Ruff, 2011). SHORT-TERM PREDICTORS OF A PROLONGED SYMPTOMATIC PERIOD POST CONCUSSION Several studies have looked at different approaches to predicting which athletes will be most likely to have a prolonged recovery (typically more than 2 weeks post injury). A study of high school and college athletes with concussions found that loss of consciousness, posttraumatic and retrograde amnesia, and greater symptom severity (an increase of 20 points or more on the Graded Symptom Checklist) within the first 24 hours following injury were associated with longer recoveries (7 or more days) (McCrea et al., 2013). The researchers also found that demographic variables, competition level (high school versus college), player position, mechanism of injury, concussion history, and acute scores on the Standardized Assessment of Concussion (SAC) and the Balance Error Scoring System (BESS) tests were not predictive of a longer recovery time (McCrea et al., 2013). Chrisman and colleagues (2013) used High School RIO™ data to identify predictors of prolonged symptoms, defined as lasting 7 or more days, in high school athletes. Presenting with four or more symptoms of concussion doubled the risk of prolonged symptoms. A history of prior concussion doubled the risk for prolonged symptoms in football players only. Symptoms of drowsiness, nausea, and concentration problems were associated with prolonged symptoms in all athletes, while sensitivity to light and noise was associated with prolonged symptoms only in non-football players. Amnesia was a risk factor only in males, and, contrary to the findings of McCrea and colleagues (2013), loss of consciousness was not a predictor of prolonged symptoms. Iverson (2007) studied 114 concussed high school football players and found that slower-to-recover concussed athletes (those taking more than 10 days to recover) were more likely to have low scores on three neuropsychological tests (visual memory, reaction time, and processing speed). Lau and colleagues (2011b) examined 107 male high school football athletes who experienced a concussion and were divided into those with rapid (defined as ≤7 days) or prolonged (≥21 days) recovery. On-field dizziness was associated with a 6.3-fold increase in the odds of a prolonged recovery. Related reports on the same sample that compared those with short (≤14 days) and prolonged (>14 days) recovery found that abnormal scores on both Immediate Post-Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT) neurocognitive testing and the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS) at 2 days after injury could identify those who would have a prolonged recovery (Lau et al., 2011a, 2012). Branch report on severity differences across concussion types

The evidence supports a distinction between mild, moderate, and severe sports-related concussions based on symptom severity, symptom duration, and objective clinical features, rather than a single categorical grade system. The strongest direct indicator in the provided material is that self-reported memory problems apparent 24 hours postconcussion were described as robust indicators of severity [N2-R1], and similar wording appears in the second excerpt from the same source [N2-R2]. This aligns with the clinical interpretation that severity is not merely about loss of consciousness or brief amnesia, but about the persistence and intensity of symptoms in the immediate aftermath of injury [N2-R1]. The Mayfield Clinic excerpt also describes a common symptom set—headache, dizziness, confusion, feeling dazed, blurred vision, nausea, and sensitivity to light or noise—and notes that “some” cases involve more serious signs [N2-R3], which suggests that severity is distinguished by the combination and presence of more alarming symptoms rather than a fixed scale.

Symptom duration and severity are the main ways mild cases differ from more severe cases. The evidence states that most young people recover within 2 weeks, while 10 to 20 percent have prolonged symptoms for weeks, months, or years [N3-F2]. A prolonged recovery is explicitly described as a constellation of physical, cognitive, emotional, and sleep symptoms beyond the usual recovery period [N3-R1], and the Mayo Clinic source defines persistent post-concussive symptoms as those lasting longer than three months [N3-R3]. The CDC/HEADS UP guidance also emphasizes that return to sports should only occur with approval from a healthcare provider, reinforcing that severity is judged by whether symptoms are still present and whether the athlete can safely resume activity [N4-R2]. In other words, mild cases are those where symptoms resolve quickly and do not interfere with normal function, whereas more severe cases are those where symptoms persist, worsen, or require medical supervision [N3-F2][N4-R2].

Features associated with longer recovery or complications include loss of consciousness, posttraumatic and retrograde amnesia, greater symptom severity, and prolonged symptom duration. The systematic review evidence notes that loss of consciousness, posttraumatic and retrograde amnesia, and a greater symptom severity increase within the first 24 hours were associated with longer recoveries [N3-F2]. It also reports that presenting with four or more symptoms of concussion doubled the risk of prolonged symptoms, and a history of prior concussion doubled the risk in football players only [N3-F2]. The same source notes that drowsiness, nausea, and concentration problems were associated with prolonged symptoms in all athletes, while sensitivity to light and noise was associated only in non-football players [N3-F2]. These findings show that severity is not uniform; some features such as amnesia and more severe early symptom burden are stronger predictors of prolonged recovery than others [N3-F2].

Baseline data and repeat injury history affect severity interpretation because prior concussion history is a known risk factor. The systematic review evidence explicitly states that a history of multiple concussions was associated with a longer recovery [N3-F2], and the AAP guidance notes that return-to-play must be individualized and that repeat injury history is part of the clinical picture [N4-F3]. The AAP consensus statement further emphasizes that return-to-play decisions are not made in isolation and must consider prior concussion history and other individual factors [N4-F3]. This means that a second concussion may appear clinically similar but is interpreted more conservatively because prior injury history increases both the likelihood of prolonged symptoms and the risk of future complications [N3-F2][N4-F3].

In summary, severity differences are best understood through symptom duration and early severity markers rather than a single clinical grade. Mild cases are typically short-lived and do not require prolonged medical supervision, while more severe cases are marked by prolonged symptoms, amnesia, greater early symptom severity, and a history of prior concussions [N2-R1][N3-F2][N4-F3]. These factors also influence whether complications or longer recovery are expected [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-F2].

Branch report on the three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions

The evidence identifies three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions: prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms, using objective tests and assessments to support decisions, and balancing immediate risk against return timelines. These concerns are clearly tied to the available sources, which emphasize symptom-based evaluation, neuropsychological testing, and the need for a cautious, individualized approach [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1].

First, clinical signs and symptoms are prioritized in decision-making because they are central to the recovery process. The systematic review evidence states that all studies of sport-related concussion use symptom reports to define recovery, and the most common measures used to define clinical recovery included somatic symptom resolution, cognitive recovery, and symptom reporting [N1-F1]. The symptom-based excerpt from the concussion severity source reinforces that self-reported memory problems 24 hours postconcussion were robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. This means that clinicians prioritize symptoms such as headache, dizziness, confusion, sensitivity to light/noise, and memory complaints because they are the most directly observable signs of ongoing impairment [N2-R3][N2-R1]. The AAP guidance also emphasizes that athletes should only return to sports with healthcare provider approval, implying that symptoms must be resolved before return is considered safe [N4-R2]. In other words, the first concern is whether the athlete still has active symptoms and whether those symptoms are consistent with continued recovery or unresolved injury [N1-F1][N4-R2].

Second, objective tests and assessments are used to support decisions because symptom reports alone are considered insufficient. The systematic review evidence reports that the most frequently used assessments were symptom reports (92%), clinical examination (86%), computerized neuropsychological testing (74%), balance testing (65%), and the Standard Assessment of Concussion (SAC) (54%) [N1-F1]. The same source also states that the CISG guidelines recommend a multifaceted evaluation including physical examination, neuropsychological testing, and a graded return to activity [N1-F1]. The baseline-testing evidence adds that baseline neurocognitive tests evaluate decision-making ability, reaction time, attention, and memory, and that baseline testing is important for concussion treatment and recovery [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The AAP guidance similarly notes that neuropsychological testing and a graded program of exertion are key components of safe return-to-play decisions [N1-R5]. This means that objective assessments are used to verify symptom resolution, cognitive recovery, balance, and baseline function, because they reduce reliance on potentially unreliable self-reporting and provide a more objective basis for timing return decisions [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2].

Third, medical judgment must balance immediate risk against return timelines because return-to-play is not a single decision but a process. The systematic review evidence emphasizes that recovery criteria are often multifaceted, and that symptom reporting alone is problematic because athletes may under-report symptoms and symptoms are not specific to concussion [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance stresses that return-to-play must be individualized and that early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time may facilitate recovery, but that any worsening symptoms should prompt a return to the previous step [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that return-to-play varies greatly in pediatric sport participants and must be individualized [N4-R4]. This reflects the third concern: clinicians must weigh the risk of premature return against the need to resume activity, using objective tests and clinical judgment to avoid early recurrence or complications while still allowing a timely return [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Overall, the three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions are: (1) prioritizing symptoms and clinical signs to identify whether recovery is ongoing, (2) using objective tests and baseline data to support the decision, and (3) balancing immediate risk with the timing of return so that the athlete is not returned too soon, but can return when medically safe [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Branch report on outcome differences and long-term consequences

The evidence supports a clear distinction between typical recovery and more persistent outcomes, with repeated or severe concussions associated with greater risk of prolonged symptoms, recurrence, and long-term consequences. Most cases resolve within 2 weeks, but some experience prolonged symptoms lasting weeks, months, or years [N3-F2]. Persistent post-concussive symptoms are defined as symptoms lasting longer than three months [N3-R3], and post-concussion syndrome is described as a constellation of physical, cognitive, emotional, and sleep symptoms beyond the usual recovery period [N3-R1]. This means that outcome differences are primarily about whether the athlete returns to baseline function within a short period or remains symptomatic beyond that [N3-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3].

Recovery patterns expected for most versus more persistent cases differ substantially. The evidence says that most young people recover within 2 weeks [N3-F2], while 10 to 20 percent have prolonged symptoms for weeks, months, or even years [N3-F2]. The systematic review evidence also notes that 15–30% of concussion patients develop persistent symptoms lasting beyond the typical recovery window [N3-R2], and that the most common definition of post-concussion syndrome is symptoms persisting beyond the usual recovery period [N3-R1]. This suggests that most cases are short-lived and recover naturally, whereas more persistent cases are marked by prolonged symptoms and functional impairment that may require ongoing management [N3-F2][N3-R2][N3-R1].

Long-term outcomes are more likely after repeated or severe concussions. The evidence states that repeated concussions are associated with an increased risk of several neurologic diseases and long-term cognitive deficits [N6-R4]. It also notes that long-term consequences can sometimes last for years [N6-R2], and that multiple concussions are linked to an increased risk of recurrence and worse outcomes [N6-R1]. The Mayo Clinic source adds that persistent post-concussive symptoms are symptoms of mild traumatic brain injury that typically last longer than three months [N3-R3], reinforcing that repeated injury history can prolong or complicate recovery [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. The AAP guidance further emphasizes that return-to-play must be individualized because recovery varies greatly [N4-R4], which supports the idea that repeated concussions alter future prognosis [N4-F3].

Return-to-play decisions can affect future risk and functional outcomes because premature return may increase the likelihood of recurrence or worse long-term consequences. The systematic review evidence states that repeat injury occurring before resolution of the first concussion is a concern because it increases the risk of more severe consequences [N1-F1]. The AAP consensus statement similarly notes that return-to-play decisions should consider repeat injury history and other individual factors [N4-F3]. This means that return decisions are not only about the current injury but also about future risk: if an athlete is returned before symptoms are fully resolved, they may be more likely to suffer another concussion, and that recurrence may worsen long-term outcomes [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence also supports that early return to activity should be supervised and cautious, with any worsening symptoms requiring a return to a prior step [N4-R3], which aligns with the idea that return timing affects future function [N4-R1][N4-R3].

In summary, outcome differences are mostly about recovery speed and persistence: most cases recover quickly, while persistent cases have prolonged symptoms and may develop post-concussion syndrome [N3-F2][N3-R1][N3-R3]. Repeated or severe concussions are associated with greater long-term risk, including neurologic diseases, cognitive deficits, and recurrence [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. Return-to-play decisions matter because they can either reduce or increase future risk, depending on whether the athlete is allowed to return while symptoms remain unresolved [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## What are the three primary concerns to consider when making return-to-play decisions after sports-related concussions?

The evidence identifies three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions:  
1) **prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms** to determine whether recovery is ongoing,  
2) **using objective tests and assessments** to support the decision, and  
3) **balancing immediate risk against return timelines** so that athletes are not returned too soon but can return when medically safe [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

### 1) Clinical signs and symptoms are prioritized in decision-making

The central idea is that symptoms are the first thing clinicians look at because they are the most directly observable indicator of ongoing impairment. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that symptom reports are central to defining recovery from sport-related concussion [N1-F1]. It also notes that self-reported memory problems apparent 24 hours postconcussion were described as robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. A broader symptom set—including headache, dizziness, confusion, feeling dazed, blurred vision, nausea, and sensitivity to light or noise—is also described as common and can signal more serious signs [N2-R3]. This means that return-to-play decisions start with the question: are the athlete’s symptoms resolving, or are they still present and active?

Clinicians also use these symptoms to monitor for worsening symptoms or complications. The systematic review evidence states that repeat injury occurring before resolution of the first concussion is a concern because it increases the risk of more severe consequences [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance adds that athletes should only return to sports with healthcare provider approval, implying that symptoms must be resolved before return is considered safe [N4-R2]. In short, the first concern is whether the athlete still has active symptoms and whether those symptoms are consistent with continued recovery or unresolved injury [N1-F1][N4-R2].

### 2) Objective tests and assessments are used to support decisions

Because symptom reports alone are considered unreliable, the evidence supports using objective tests and assessments as a second layer of evaluation. The systematic review evidence reports that the most frequently used assessments were symptom reports (92%), clinical examination (86%), computerized neuropsychological testing (74%), balance testing (65%), and the Standard Assessment of Concussion (SAC) (54%) [N1-F1]. It also states that the CISG guidelines recommend a multifaceted evaluation including physical examination, neuropsychological testing, and a graded return to activity [N1-F1]. The baseline-testing evidence adds that baseline neurocognitive tests evaluate decision-making ability, reaction time, attention, and memory, and that baseline testing is important for concussion treatment and recovery [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The AAP guidance similarly notes that neuropsychological testing and a graded program of exertion are key components of safe return-to-play decisions [N1-R5].

These objective tests matter because they help verify whether symptoms are real and whether cognitive, balance, or other functions have returned to baseline. The evidence explicitly says that all studies of sport-related concussion use symptom reports to define recovery, but that symptom reporting alone is problematic because athletes may under-report symptoms and symptoms are not specific to concussion [N1-F1]. That is why objective testing is used to support the decision, not replace it [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2].

### 3) Medical judgment balances immediate risk versus return timelines

Return-to-play is not a single decision but a process. The evidence emphasizes that recovery criteria are often multifaceted, and that clinicians must weigh the risk of premature return against the need to resume activity [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance stresses that return-to-play must be individualized, and that early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time may facilitate recovery, but that any worsening symptoms should prompt a return to the previous step [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that return-to-play varies greatly in pediatric sport participants and must be individualized [N4-R4].

This means the third concern is not just whether the athlete can play, but when it is safe to play. Clinicians must avoid returning an athlete too soon, because premature return may increase the likelihood of recurrence or worse long-term consequences [N1-F1][N4-F3]. At the same time, they must not delay return unnecessarily, because prolonged inactivity can also have negative effects on function and recovery [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The balance is therefore between minimizing immediate risk and allowing a timely, medically supervised return [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

## How do severity and outcomes differ?

The evidence supports a clear distinction between mild, moderate, and severe concussions based on symptom severity, symptom duration, and objective clinical features, rather than a single categorical grade system. Self-reported memory problems apparent 24 hours postconcussion were described as robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. The Mayfield Clinic excerpt also describes a common symptom set and notes that “some” cases involve more serious signs [N2-R3], which suggests that severity is distinguished by the combination and presence of more alarming symptoms rather than a fixed scale [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Mild cases versus more severe cases

Most cases are mild in the sense that symptoms resolve quickly. The evidence states that most young people recover within 2 weeks, while 10 to 20 percent have prolonged symptoms for weeks, months, or even years [N3-F2]. A prolonged recovery is explicitly described as a constellation of physical, cognitive, emotional, and sleep symptoms beyond the usual recovery period [N3-R1]. The Mayo Clinic source defines persistent post-concussive symptoms as those lasting longer than three months [N3-R3]. This means that mild cases are those where symptoms resolve quickly and do not interfere with normal function, whereas more severe cases are those where symptoms persist, worsen, or require medical supervision [N3-F2][N4-R2].

### Features associated with longer recovery or complications

Several features are associated with longer recovery or complications. The systematic review evidence notes that loss of consciousness, posttraumatic and retrograde amnesia, and greater symptom severity within the first 24 hours were associated with longer recoveries [N3-F2]. It also reports that presenting with four or more symptoms of concussion doubled the risk of prolonged symptoms, and a history of prior concussion doubled the risk in football players only [N3-F2]. The same source notes that drowsiness, nausea, and concentration problems were associated with prolonged symptoms in all athletes, while sensitivity to light and noise was associated only in non-football players [N3-F2]. These findings show that severity is not uniform; some features such as amnesia and more severe early symptom burden are stronger predictors of prolonged recovery than others [N3-F2].

### How baseline data and repeat injury history affect severity interpretation

Baseline data and repeat injury history affect severity interpretation because prior concussion history is a known risk factor. The systematic review evidence explicitly states that a history of multiple concussions was associated with a longer recovery [N3-F2], and the AAP guidance notes that return-to-play must be individualized and that repeat injury history is part of the clinical picture [N4-F3]. The AAP consensus statement further emphasizes that return-to-play decisions are not made in isolation and must consider prior concussion history and other individual factors [N4-F3]. This means that a second concussion may appear clinically similar but is interpreted more conservatively because prior injury history increases both the likelihood of prolonged symptoms and the risk of future complications [N3-F2][N4-F3].

## How do return-to-play decisions affect future risk and long-term outcomes?

The evidence shows that return-to-play decisions can influence future risk and functional outcomes. The systematic review evidence explicitly states that repeat injury occurring before resolution of the first concussion is a concern because it increases the risk of more severe consequences [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance similarly notes that return-to-play must be individualized and that prior concussion history should be considered [N4-F3]. This means that premature return can increase the likelihood of recurrence, while a cautious, supervised return may reduce that risk [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Long-term outcomes are more likely after repeated or severe concussions. The evidence states that repeated concussions are associated with an increased risk of several neurologic diseases and long-term cognitive deficits [N6-R4]. It also notes that long-term consequences can sometimes last for years [N6-R2], and that multiple concussions are linked to an increased risk of recurrence and worse outcomes [N6-R1]. The Mayo Clinic source adds that persistent post-concussive symptoms are symptoms of mild traumatic brain injury that typically last longer than three months [N3-R3], reinforcing that repeated injury history can prolong or complicate recovery [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

## Summary

In short, the three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions are:  
1) **prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms** to determine whether recovery is ongoing,  
2) **using objective tests and assessments** to support the decision, and  
3) **balancing immediate risk against return timelines** so that athletes are not returned too soon but can return when medically safe [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Severity and outcomes differ because mild cases typically resolve quickly, while more severe cases are marked by prolonged symptoms, amnesia, greater early symptom severity, and a history of prior concussions [N2-R1][N3-F2][N4-F3]. Long-term outcomes are more likely after repeated or severe concussions, including persistent symptoms, post-concussion syndrome, neurologic diseases, and cognitive deficits [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. Return-to-play decisions matter because they can either reduce or increase future risk, depending on whether the athlete is returned while symptoms remain unresolved [N1-F1][N4-F3].

The evidence identifies three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions: prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms, using objective tests and assessments to support decisions, and balancing immediate risk against return timelines. The symptom-based excerpt from the concussion severity source reinforces that self-reported memory problems 24 hours postconcussion were robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. Second, objective tests and assessments are used to support decisions because symptom reports alone are considered insufficient. The systematic review evidence reports that the most frequently used assessments were symptom reports (92%), clinical examination (86%), computerized neuropsychological testing (74%), balance testing (65%), and the Standard Assessment of Concussion (SAC) (54%) [N1-F1]. Third, medical judgment must balance immediate risk against return timelines because return-to-play is not a single decision but a process. ## What are the three primary concerns to consider when making return-to-play decisions after sports-related concussions?

The evidence identifies three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions:  
1) **prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms** to determine whether recovery is ongoing,  
2) **using objective tests and assessments** to support the decision, and  
3) **balancing immediate risk against return timelines** so that athletes are not returned too soon but can return when medically safe [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

### 1) Clinical signs and symptoms are prioritized in decision-making

The central idea is that symptoms are the first thing clinicians look at because they are the most directly observable indicator of ongoing impairment. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that symptom reports are central to defining recovery from sport-related concussion [N1-F1]. It also notes that self-reported memory problems apparent 24 hours postconcussion were described as robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. A broader symptom set—including headache, dizziness, confusion, feeling dazed, blurred vision, nausea, and sensitivity to light or noise—is also described as common and can signal more serious signs [N2-R3]. This means that return-to-play decisions start with the question: are the athlete’s symptoms resolving, or are they still present and active?

Clinicians also use these symptoms to monitor for worsening symptoms or complications. The systematic review evidence states that repeat injury occurring before resolution of the first concussion is a concern because it increases the risk of more severe consequences [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance adds that athletes should only return to sports with healthcare provider approval, implying that symptoms must be resolved before return is considered safe [N4-R2]. In short, the first concern is whether the athlete still has active symptoms and whether those symptoms are consistent with continued recovery or unresolved injury [N1-F1][N4-R2].

### 2) Objective tests and assessments are used to support decisions

Because symptom reports alone are considered unreliable, the evidence supports using objective tests and assessments as a second layer of evaluation. The systematic review evidence reports that the most frequently used assessments were symptom reports (92%), clinical examination (86%), computerized neuropsychological testing (74%), balance testing (65%), and the Standard Assessment of Concussion (SAC) (54%) [N1-F1]. It also states that the CISG guidelines recommend a multifaceted evaluation including physical examination, neuropsychological testing, and a graded return to activity [N1-F1]. The baseline-testing evidence adds that baseline neurocognitive tests evaluate decision-making ability, reaction time, attention, and memory, and that baseline testing is important for concussion treatment and recovery [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The AAP guidance similarly notes that neuropsychological testing and a graded program of exertion are key components of safe return-to-play decisions [N1-R5].

These objective tests matter because they help verify whether symptoms are real and whether cognitive, balance, or other functions have returned to baseline. The evidence explicitly says that all studies of sport-related concussion use symptom reports to define recovery, but that symptom reporting alone is problematic because athletes may under-report symptoms and symptoms are not specific to concussion [N1-F1]. That is why objective testing is used to support the decision, not replace it [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2].

### 3) Medical judgment balances immediate risk versus return timelines

Return-to-play is not a single decision but a process. The evidence emphasizes that recovery criteria are often multifaceted, and that clinicians must weigh the risk of premature return against the need to resume activity [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance stresses that return-to-play must be individualized, and that early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time may facilitate recovery, but that any worsening symptoms should prompt a return to the previous step [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that return-to-play varies greatly in pediatric sport participants and must be individualized [N4-R4].

This means the third concern is not just whether the athlete can play, but when it is safe to play. Clinicians must avoid returning an athlete too soon, because premature return may increase the likelihood of recurrence or worse long-term consequences [N1-F1][N4-F3]. At the same time, they must not delay return unnecessarily, because prolonged inactivity can also have negative effects on function and recovery [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The balance is therefore between minimizing immediate risk and allowing a timely, medically supervised return [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

## How do severity and outcomes differ?

The evidence supports a clear distinction between mild, moderate, and severe concussions based on symptom severity, symptom duration, and objective clinical features, rather than a single categorical grade system. Self-reported memory problems apparent 24 hours postconcussion were described as robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. The Mayfield Clinic excerpt also describes a common symptom set and notes that “some” cases involve more serious signs [N2-R3], which suggests that severity is distinguished by the combination and presence of more alarming symptoms rather than a fixed scale [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Mild cases versus more severe cases

Most cases are mild in the sense that symptoms resolve quickly. The evidence states that most young people recover within 2 weeks, while 10 to 20 percent have prolonged symptoms for weeks, months, or even years [N3-F2]. A prolonged recovery is explicitly described as a constellation of physical, cognitive, emotional, and sleep symptoms beyond the usual recovery period [N3-R1]. The Mayo Clinic source defines persistent post-concussive symptoms as those lasting longer than three months [N3-R3]. This means that mild cases are those where symptoms resolve quickly and do not interfere with normal function, whereas more severe cases are those where symptoms persist, worsen, or require medical supervision [N3-F2][N4-R2].

### Features associated with longer recovery or complications

Several features are associated with longer recovery or complications. The systematic review evidence notes that loss of consciousness, posttraumatic and retrograde amnesia, and greater symptom severity within the first 24 hours were associated with longer recoveries [N3-F2]. It also reports that presenting with four or more symptoms of concussion doubled the risk of prolonged symptoms, and a history of prior concussion doubled the risk in football players only [N3-F2]. The same source notes that drowsiness, nausea, and concentration problems were associated with prolonged symptoms in all athletes, while sensitivity to light and noise was associated only in non-football players [N3-F2]. These findings show that severity is not uniform; some features such as amnesia and more severe early symptom burden are stronger predictors of prolonged recovery than others [N3-F2].

Baseline data and repeat injury history affect severity interpretation because prior concussion history is a known risk factor. This means that a second concussion may appear clinically similar but is interpreted more conservatively because prior injury history increases both the likelihood of prolonged symptoms and the risk of future complications [N3-F2][N4-F3].

The evidence shows that return-to-play decisions can influence future risk and functional outcomes. Long-term outcomes are more likely after repeated or severe concussions. 1) **prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms** to determine whether recovery is ongoing,  
2) **using objective tests and assessments** to support the decision, and  
3) **balancing immediate risk against return timelines** so that athletes are not returned too soon but can return when medically safe [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Long-term outcomes are more likely after repeated or severe concussions, including persistent symptoms, post-concussion syndrome, neurologic diseases, and cognitive deficits [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. ## What are the three primary concerns to consider when making return-to-play decisions after sports-related concussions?

The evidence identifies three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions:  
1) **prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms** to determine whether recovery is ongoing,  
2) **using objective tests and assessments** to support the decision, and  
3) **balancing immediate risk against return timelines** so that athletes are not returned too soon but can return when medically safe [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

### 1) Clinical signs and symptoms are prioritized in decision-making

The central idea is that symptoms are the first thing clinicians look at because they are the most directly observable indicator of ongoing impairment. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that symptom reports are central to defining recovery from sport-related concussion [N1-F1]. It also notes that self-reported memory problems apparent 24 hours postconcussion were described as robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. A broader symptom set—including headache, dizziness, confusion, feeling dazed, blurred vision, nausea, and sensitivity to light or noise—is also described as common and can signal more serious signs [N2-R3]. This means that return-to-play decisions start with the question: are the athlete’s symptoms resolving, or are they still present and active?

Clinicians also use these symptoms to monitor for worsening symptoms or complications. The systematic review evidence states that repeat injury occurring before resolution of the first concussion is a concern because it increases the risk of more severe consequences [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance adds that athletes should only return to sports with healthcare provider approval, implying that symptoms must be resolved before return is considered safe [N4-R2]. In short, the first concern is whether the athlete still has active symptoms and whether those symptoms are consistent with continued recovery or unresolved injury [N1-F1][N4-R2].

### 2) Objective tests and assessments are used to support decisions

Because symptom reports alone are considered unreliable, the evidence supports using objective tests and assessments as a second layer of evaluation. The systematic review evidence reports that the most frequently used assessments were symptom reports (92%), clinical examination (86%), computerized neuropsychological testing (74%), balance testing (65%), and the Standard Assessment of Concussion (SAC) (54%) [N1-F1]. It also states that the CISG guidelines recommend a multifaceted evaluation including physical examination, neuropsychological testing, and a graded return to activity [N1-F1]. The baseline-testing evidence adds that baseline neurocognitive tests evaluate decision-making ability, reaction time, attention, and memory, and that baseline testing is important for concussion treatment and recovery [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The AAP guidance similarly notes that neuropsychological testing and a graded program of exertion are key components of safe return-to-play decisions [N1-R5].

These objective tests matter because they help verify whether symptoms are real and whether cognitive, balance, or other functions have returned to baseline. The evidence explicitly says that all studies of sport-related concussion use symptom reports to define recovery, but that symptom reporting alone is problematic because athletes may under-report symptoms and symptoms are not specific to concussion [N1-F1]. That is why objective testing is used to support the decision, not replace it [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2].

### 3) Medical judgment balances immediate risk versus return timelines

Return-to-play is not a single decision but a process. The evidence emphasizes that recovery criteria are often multifaceted, and that clinicians must weigh the risk of premature return against the need to resume activity [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance stresses that return-to-play must be individualized, and that early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time may facilitate recovery, but that any worsening symptoms should prompt a return to the previous step [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that return-to-play varies greatly in pediatric sport participants and must be individualized [N4-R4].

This means the third concern is not just whether the athlete can play, but when it is safe to play. Clinicians must avoid returning an athlete too soon, because premature return may increase the likelihood of recurrence or worse long-term consequences [N1-F1][N4-F3]. At the same time, they must not delay return unnecessarily, because prolonged inactivity can also have negative effects on function and recovery [N4-R1][N4-R3]. The balance is therefore between minimizing immediate risk and allowing a timely, medically supervised return [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

## How do severity and outcomes differ?

The evidence supports a clear distinction between mild, moderate, and severe concussions based on symptom severity, symptom duration, and objective clinical features, rather than a single categorical grade system. Self-reported memory problems apparent 24 hours postconcussion were described as robust indicators of severity [N2-R1]. The Mayfield Clinic excerpt also describes a common symptom set and notes that “some” cases involve more serious signs [N2-R3], which suggests that severity is distinguished by the combination and presence of more alarming symptoms rather than a fixed scale [N2-R1][N2-R3].

### Mild cases versus more severe cases

Most cases are mild in the sense that symptoms resolve quickly. The evidence states that most young people recover within 2 weeks, while 10 to 20 percent have prolonged symptoms for weeks, months, or even years [N3-F2]. A prolonged recovery is explicitly described as a constellation of physical, cognitive, emotional, and sleep symptoms beyond the usual recovery period [N3-R1]. The Mayo Clinic source defines persistent post-concussive symptoms as those lasting longer than three months [N3-R3]. This means that mild cases are those where symptoms resolve quickly and do not interfere with normal function, whereas more severe cases are those where symptoms persist, worsen, or require medical supervision [N3-F2][N4-R2].

Several features are associated with longer recovery or complications. The systematic review evidence notes that loss of consciousness, posttraumatic and retrograde amnesia, and greater symptom severity within the first 24 hours were associated with longer recoveries [N3-F2]. It also reports that presenting with four or more symptoms of concussion doubled the risk of prolonged symptoms, and a history of prior concussion doubled the risk in football players only [N3-F2]. The same source notes that drowsiness, nausea, and concentration problems were associated with prolonged symptoms in all athletes, while sensitivity to light and noise was associated only in non-football players [N3-F2]. These findings show that severity is not uniform; some features such as amnesia and more severe early symptom burden are stronger predictors of prolonged recovery than others [N3-F2].

Baseline data and repeat injury history affect severity interpretation because prior concussion history is a known risk factor. The systematic review evidence explicitly states that a history of multiple concussions was associated with a longer recovery [N3-F2], and the AAP guidance notes that return-to-play must be individualized and that repeat injury history is part of the clinical picture [N4-F3]. The AAP consensus statement further emphasizes that return-to-play decisions are not made in isolation and must consider prior concussion history and other individual factors [N4-F3]. This means that a second concussion may appear clinically similar but is interpreted more conservatively because prior injury history increases both the likelihood of prolonged symptoms and the risk of future complications [N3-F2][N4-F3].

The evidence shows that return-to-play decisions can influence future risk and functional outcomes. The systematic review evidence explicitly states that repeat injury occurring before resolution of the first concussion is a concern because it increases the risk of more severe consequences [N1-F1]. The AAP guidance similarly notes that return-to-play must be individualized and that prior concussion history should be considered [N4-F3]. This means that premature return can increase the likelihood of recurrence, while a cautious, supervised return may reduce that risk [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Long-term outcomes are more likely after repeated or severe concussions. The evidence states that repeated concussions are associated with an increased risk of several neurologic diseases and long-term cognitive deficits [N6-R4]. It also notes that long-term consequences can sometimes last for years [N6-R2], and that multiple concussions are linked to an increased risk of recurrence and worse outcomes [N6-R1]. In short, the three primary concerns in return-to-play decisions are:  
1) **prioritizing clinical signs and symptoms** to determine whether recovery is ongoing,  
2) **using objective tests and assessments** to support the decision, and  
3) **balancing immediate risk against return timelines** so that athletes are not returned too soon but can return when medically safe [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-R1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Long-term outcomes are more likely after repeated or severe concussions, including persistent symptoms, post-concussion syndrome, neurologic diseases, and cognitive deficits [N3-R1][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].
